stories.title: Amit's Poker Journey
stories.description: Amit shares his experience playing poker seriously between 2010 and 2015, including writing a column for the Economic Times. He eventually left because he realized that the skills that make you good at poker (math, discipline) are transferable to other fields where you don't have to deal with the high variance and emotional toll of gambling.

stories.title: The Coin Toss EV Example
stories.description: Amit explains Expected Value (EV) using a coin toss. If someone offers you 51 paise for heads and takes 49 paise for tails, it's a +EV bet (1 paisa per toss). Even if you lose (tails), it was the right decision. This illustrates process over results.

stories.title: Ace Ten of Hearts
stories.description: A thought experiment where you have Ace-Ten of hearts and need one more heart to win. Amit calculates the pot odds (2 to 1) vs. the odds of hitting the flush (approx 2 to 1 against) to determine if a call is +EV.

stories.title: Entitlement Tilt
stories.description: Amit confesses to suffering from 'entitlement tilt'—getting angry when a 'bad' player (who plays like it's Teen Patti on Diwali) beats his 'correct' play with dumb luck. This emotional loss of control leads to bad decisions and losing money.

stories.title: Why Bad Players Don't Bet on Chess
stories.description: Ajay asks why bad players bet on poker but not chess. Amit explains that chess gives immediate, accurate feedback (you lose). Poker has high variance; bad players can win in the short term, leading to the delusion that they are skilled.

core_ideas.description: The most critical concept in poker and life. It's not about winning every hand, but about making decisions that have a positive average outcome over time. 'If you keep making +EV decisions, you will be a winner in the long run.'
You can make the right decision and still lose (get unlucky). You can make the wrong decision and win (get lucky). Don't judge the quality of a decision by its outcome. Focus on the process (Dharma).
The world is not deterministic (0% or 100%). Everything is a probability. Acknowledging this helps in making better decisions and maintaining equanimity.

GTO is playing a mathematically unexploitable strategy (perfect balance). Exploitative play involves identifying opponents' mistakes and deviating from GTO to take advantage of them, which in turn makes you exploitable.
Mastering the math is not enough; you must master your mind. 'Tilt' is when emotions (anger, ego, loss aversion) cause you to make sub-optimal decisions.

Because luck plays a huge role in the short term, skill only manifests over a large sample size. You must 'put in volume' (play many hands, take many small bets) to let the law of large numbers work in your favor.
We look at the past and think events were inevitable. In reality, they were just one of many possible paths that happened to materialize.
